title: 2012 HMMT February Guts Problem 18
statement: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be positive real numbers such that \(x^{2}+y^{2}=1\) and \(\left(3 x-4 x^{3}\right)\left(3 y-4 y^{3}\right)=-\frac{1}{2}\). Compute \(x+y\).

solutions.text: \(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}\) Solution 1: Let \(x=\cos (\theta)\) and \(y=\sin (\theta)\). Then, by the triple angle formulae, we have that \(3 x-4 x^{3}=-\cos (3 \theta)\) and \(3 y-4 y^{3}=\sin (3 \theta)\), so \(-\sin (3 \theta) \cos (3 \theta)=-\frac{1}{2}\). We can write this as \(2 \sin (3 \theta) \cos (3 \theta)=\sin (6 \theta)=1\), so \(\theta=\frac{1}{6} \sin ^{-1}(1)=\frac{\pi}{12}\). Thus, \(x+y=\cos \left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right)+\sin \left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right)=\) \(\frac{\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{2}}{4}+\frac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4}=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}\).
